chapters.title: Chapter 2: Cyclical, Defensive, and Growth Sectors

lessons.title: The Cyclical P/E Trap: Why Cheap Can Mean Peak Earnings

body.text: For a cyclical company, a very low P/E is often a warning, not a bargain. It usually means earnings are at their peak and the market expects them to fall. A very high P/E often means earnings are at the bottom. Read P/E the normal way in a cyclical sector and you will buy at the top and sell at the bottom.

children.text: You now know that cyclical earnings swing hard, and that operating leverage makes the swings even bigger. This lesson shows the most expensive consequence of that for retail investors: the P/E ratio, the most used valuation number on Screener.in, gives backwards signals in cyclical sectors. Many investors have bought a metal or commodity stock at a P/E of 4 because it 'looked cheap', only to watch it halve.

P/E divides today's price by recent earnings. The price looks forward, pricing in what investors expect over many years. The earnings look backward, showing only the last twelve months. For a steady business, the two stay roughly in sync. For a cyclical business at the top of its cycle, recent earnings are unusually high while the price already reflects an expected decline, so the P/E looks tiny. At the bottom, earnings are unusually low while the price reflects an expected recovery, so the P/E looks huge. The legendary US fund manager Peter Lynch popularised this idea: with cyclicals, be wary of the low P/E and pay attention when the P/E looks too high.

body.caption: An Illustrative Steel Company Through One Full Cycle

body.title: Illustrative Steel Company: Reported P/E Through the Cycle

children.text: Look at the shape. The P/E hits its lowest point, 6, at exactly the moment earnings peak. It hits its highest point, 44, when earnings are near zero. An investor who bought in Year 1 at a scary-looking P/E of 25 and sold in Year 3 at a 'cheap' P/E of 6 more than doubled their money. An investor who did the opposite, following the textbook rule, lost heavily.

body.title: The Cost of Buying the 'Cheap' P/E
body.prompt: Pooja buys the illustrative steel company in Year 3 at ₹600 because its P/E of 6 looks like a bargain. She holds on until Year 5, when the price is ₹220. What percentage of her investment has she lost? Enter the loss as a positive number, rounded to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Loss = (600 - 220) ÷ 600 = 380 ÷ 600 = 63.3%. Compare the investor who bought at ₹250 in Year 1 when the P/E was 25 and sold at ₹600 in Year 3: a gain of (600 - 250) ÷ 250 = 140%. Same stock, same cycle; the P/E signal pointed the wrong way both times.

markDefs.definition: An estimate of what a company earns in an average year, calculated by averaging earnings across a full business cycle rather than using a single boom or bust year.

children.text: Instead of dividing the price by one year's earnings, divide it by

: the average EPS across a complete cycle, typically five to ten years. This strips out the boom and the bust and asks a better question: how much am I paying for this company's earnings power in a normal year?

body.latex: \text{Normalised P/E} = \frac{\text{Current share price}}{\text{Average EPS over a full cycle}} \qquad \text{Average EPS} = \frac{10 + 40 + 100 + 30 + 5}{5} = \text{₹37}
body.caption: Normalised P/E, with the illustrative steel company's five-year average EPS

children.text: Normalised P/E puts the signals back the right way round. At the peak, the stock that looked cheap at 6 is actually expensive at 16.2. At the trough, the stock that looked expensive at 25 is actually cheap at 6.8. One caution: this only works in hindsight when you know the full cycle. In real time, use as many past years as Screener.in shows, and make sure the period includes at least one genuine downturn.

body.title: Calculate the Normalised P/E
body.prompt: In Year 4, the illustrative steel company trades at ₹330. Its reported P/E is 11. Using the five-year average EPS of ₹37, what is its normalised P/E? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: Normalised P/E = ₹330 ÷ ₹37 = 8.9. The reported P/E of 11 overstates how expensive the stock is, because Year 4's EPS of ₹30 is still below the cycle average as earnings slide into the downturn.

children.text: Reading the Cycle: Peak Signals vs Trough Signals

body.title: What the Top and Bottom of a Cycle Usually Look Like

columns.label: Signs of a peak
points: Operating margins far above the company's ten-year average
Commodity or product prices at or near record highs
Several companies in the industry announcing large capacity expansions at once
Reported P/E looks very low and dividends look very generous
Analysts and business channels extrapolating record profits into future years

columns.label: Signs of a trough
points: Margins far below average, losses, or dividend cuts
Product prices near or below the cost of the weaker producers
Capacity expansions cancelled, plants shut, weaker players selling out or going bankrupt
Reported P/E very high or not meaningful because earnings are negative
Widespread pessimism and very little institutional interest in the sector

body.title: Which Is the Biggest Warning Sign?
body.question: A cement company trades at a P/E of 9, well below its usual range. Which additional fact should worry you most about buying it now?
options: Its operating margin this year is double its ten-year average, and four large competitors have announced major new plants
It paid a lower dividend last year than the year before
Its P/E is higher than a steel company's P/E
Its share price has fallen 10% from its 52-week high
body.explanation: Margins far above the long-run average combined with an industry-wide capacity build-up are classic peak signals. New supply tends to arrive just as demand cools, pushing prices and margins back down. The low P/E is likely reflecting peak earnings, not a bargain. The other facts say little about where the cycle stands.

body.title: Indian case study: steel after the 2021 to 2022 boom

content.title: How a Record Year Turned Into a Sharp Earnings Fall

events.title: Steel prices surge
events.description: Post-lockdown demand recovery, supply disruptions, and a global commodity rally pushed steel prices to record levels. Indian steelmakers' margins expanded sharply.

events.title: Record profits, low P/E
events.description: Tata Steel reported record consolidated net profit of over ₹40,000 crore for the year ending March 2022. On those earnings, its reported P/E looked very low.

events.title: Export duty imposed
events.description: The government imposed an export duty on several steel products to cool domestic prices, hitting realisations for exporters. Steel stocks fell sharply.

events.title: Duty withdrawn
events.description: The export duty was rolled back as global steel prices had already cooled.

events.title: Profits fall by around 80%
events.description: With steel prices down and input costs still high, Tata Steel's consolidated net profit fell to roughly ₹8,000 crore for the year ending March 2023. The 'cheap' P/E of the previous year had been built on peak earnings.

content.text: The lesson is not that steel stocks were a bad investment. It is that a single record year's earnings told you almost nothing about the next year's, and a P/E built on those earnings was misleading.

body.title: The Stock Tip at the Family Dinner
body.scenario: At a family dinner, your uncle recommends an aluminium company. 'It trades at a P/E of just 5, the dividend yield is 7%, and profits have tripled in two years. Screener.in shows it is one of the cheapest stocks in the Nifty 500. It's a no-brainer.'
body.prompt: What would you check before agreeing with him?
body.modelAnswer: Every fact he mentions is consistent with a cyclical peak. Profits tripling in two years in a commodity business usually means aluminium prices have surged, not that the company has permanently improved. A 7% dividend yield and a P/E of 5 both depend on this year's earnings holding up. Check: How do current operating margins compare with the ten-year average on Screener.in? Where are global aluminium prices relative to their long-term range? Is the industry adding capacity? What is the normalised P/E using average EPS over all the years Screener.in shows? What would the P/E be if earnings fell back to the cycle average? If margins are far above normal, the stock may be fairly or even fully valued despite looking cheap.

body.text: Screener.in's default screens sort by reported P/E. A 'low P/E' screen run during a commodity boom will be full of metals, mining, shipping, and sugar stocks at their earnings peaks. Always exclude or separately review cyclicals when screening on P/E.

body.title: Fill in the Blank
body.textWithBlank: For cyclical companies, dividing today's price by average EPS across a full business cycle gives you a ___ P/E, which avoids being misled by boom or bust years.
body.explanation: Normalised P/E uses average earnings over a full cycle, so it does not look artificially cheap at the peak or artificially expensive at the trough.

body.title: Before You Buy a Cyclical Because It Looks Cheap
steps: Confirm the company is in a cyclical sector using the spectrum from the previous lessons
Pull every year of EPS that Screener.in shows and check that the period includes at least one downturn
Calculate average EPS across those years and divide the current price by it to get normalised P/E
Compare the current operating margin with its long-run average; far above average suggests a peak
Check whether product prices are near record highs and whether the industry is adding a lot of new capacity
Ask what the stock would be worth if earnings returned to the cycle average, not what it is worth if this year repeats

points: For cyclical companies, P/E tends to be lowest at peak earnings and highest at trough earnings, the opposite of what the textbook rule suggests
The price looks forward while reported earnings look backward, which is why the ratio flips in cyclical sectors
Normalised P/E, price divided by average EPS across a full cycle, puts the valuation signal back the right way round
Peak signals include record margins, record product prices, and industry-wide capacity expansion; trough signals include losses, plant closures, and deep pessimism
Indian steel in 2021 to 2023 showed how a record year's low P/E can come just before a sharp fall in profits
Low P/E screens during commodity booms fill up with cyclicals at their peak; review them separately

body.text: The steel company example is illustrative. Figures for Tata Steel are approximate and quoted for educational purposes only; refer to the company's published results for exact numbers. Nothing in this lesson is a recommendation to buy or sell any security.
